title: The Reform Edict of 1856: Ottoman Modernisation
shortDesc: The Islahat Fermanı of February 1856 extended formal legal equality to the empire's non-Muslim subjects and accelerated the Tanzimat programme of administrative and institutional modernisation (Davison, 1963). In Istanbul the reform era manifested spatially through new municipal institutions, European-style building regulations, and the gradual transformation of Galata and Pera into a Westernised commercial quarter.

title: The Second Constitutional Era
shortDesc: The Young Turk Revolution of July 1908 compelled Abdülhamid II to restore the 1876 constitution, ending three decades of autocratic rule and inaugurating an era of mass politics in the imperial capital (Hanioğlu, 2008). Istanbul's public sphere expanded rapidly through a liberated press, political associations, and street demonstrations that redefined the city's civic spaces.

title: Allied Occupation of Constantinople
shortDesc: Following the Armistice of Mudros, Allied fleets anchored off the Golden Horn on 13 November 1918, initiating an occupation that placed the Ottoman capital under foreign military administration until 1923 (Criss, 1999). The occupation years brought demographic upheaval — including the influx of White Russian refugees — and stimulated the nationalist resistance movement that would relocate political authority to Anatolia.

title: Proclamation of the Republic: Istanbul After Empire
shortDesc: The proclamation of the Turkish Republic on 29 October 1923, with Ankara as its capital, ended Istanbul's sixteen-century role as an imperial seat (Zürcher, 2004). Deprived of court, ministries, and diplomatic corps, the city entered a period of relative demographic and economic stagnation that lasted until mid-century industrialisation reversed its fortunes.

title: The September 1955 Pogrom
shortDesc: On 6–7 September 1955, organised riots devastated Greek, Armenian, and Jewish properties across Istanbul, damaging thousands of shops, homes, and religious buildings (Güven, 2011). The pogrom accelerated the emigration of the city's remaining non-Muslim communities, fundamentally altering the demographic and commercial character of districts such as Beyoğlu.

title: The Bosphorus Bridge: Linking Two Continents
shortDesc: The Bosphorus Bridge, opened on the Republic's fiftieth anniversary in 1973, established the first fixed road crossing between the European and Asian shores (Gül, 2009). The bridge redirected metropolitan growth toward the Anatolian side and, together with its successors, entrenched an automobile-oriented development pattern that continues to shape the city's expansion.

title: The 1999 Marmara Earthquake
shortDesc: The magnitude 7.6 İzmit earthquake of 17 August 1999 killed more than 17,000 people across the Marmara region and exposed systemic deficiencies in Turkey's building production and inspection regimes (Özerdem & Jacoby, 2006). The disaster catalysed revisions to seismic codes and placed the vulnerability of Istanbul's building stock — much of it unengineered — at the centre of national policy debate.

title: Opening of EU Accession Negotiations
shortDesc: Turkey's accession negotiations with the European Union, formally opened on 3 October 2005, followed a decade of political and legal reforms undertaken to meet the Copenhagen criteria (Müftüler-Baç, 2005). For Istanbul the process reinforced integration with European markets and institutions, sustaining the foreign investment inflows that underwrote the decade's construction boom.

title: European Capital of Culture 2010
shortDesc: Istanbul's designation as European Capital of Culture for 2010, shared with Pécs and Essen, framed the city as a bridge between European and Ottoman-Islamic heritages (Göktürk, Soysal, & Türeli, 2010). The programme channelled investment into museums and heritage restoration while provoking scholarly debate over culture-led regeneration and its displacement effects in historic neighbourhoods.
